contrasts.title: The verb comes second
contrasts.body: In a Norwegian main clause the verb is always the second element. If you start with a time or place, the subject moves after the verb: «I dag er det min første dag», not «I dag det er…».

contrasts.title: «Halv tolv» is 11:30
contrasts.body: Norwegian counts half an hour towards the next hour. «Halv tolv» means 11:30, not 12:30 as British «half twelve» would.

contrasts.title: «Ikke» before the verb after «fordi»
contrasts.body: In a main clause «ikke» comes after the verb: «Trikken går ikke». After «fordi», «at» or «hvis» it moves in front of the verb: «…fordi trikken ikke går».

contrasts.title: «Toroms» counts all rooms
contrasts.body: Flat ads count the living room too. A «toromsleilighet» has two rooms: a living room and one bedroom. A «treroms» has two bedrooms.

contrasts.title: Words in the exercises
contrasts.body: The instructions are in simple Norwegian, and they repeat. «Hvilket ord hører du?» Which word do you hear? «Hvilken bokstav hører du?» Which letter do you hear? «Hva svarer du?» What do you answer? «Skriv det du hører.» Write what you hear. «Lag en setning.» Make a sentence.

contrasts.title: How æ, ø and å sound
contrasts.body: æ is close to the a in «bad», said longer. ø is like the vowel in «fur» with rounded lips. å is like the aw in «law». Careful with o: in Norwegian it often sounds like the oo in «food», so «bor» sounds close to «boor».

contrasts.title: Two sounds English spells «sh» and «h»
contrasts.body: kj, and k before i, y or ei, is a soft hiss like the h in «huge»: kjøre, kino. sj, skj, and sk before i, y or øy, sound like «sh»: sju, skje, ski. gj and hj are just a y sound: gjøre, hjem.

contrasts.title: Double consonant, short vowel
contrasts.body: A double consonant makes the vowel before it short: «takk» (thanks) has a short a, «tak» (roof) a long one. The same goes for «penn» (pen) and «pen» (pretty). Getting the length right matters more than the exact vowel.

contrasts.title: Letters you write but don’t say
contrasts.body: The h in hv- and hj- is silent: hva, hvor, hjem. A final d after a vowel is often silent: god, med, ved. And «jeg» is said «yai».

contrasts.title: Everyone is «du»
contrasts.body: Norwegian uses «du» (you) for everyone: your boss, the doctor, a stranger in the street. The formal «De» is almost never used, so you never have to choose.

contrasts.title: There is no everyday word for «please»
contrasts.body: Politeness comes from the question and from thanking. «Kan jeg få en kaffe?» (Can I have a coffee?) and «Jeg vil gjerne ha…» (I would like…) are polite on their own. Add «takk» at the end: «En kaffe, takk.»

contrasts.title: førti or fjorten?
contrasts.body: -ti marks the tens and -ten the teens: førti 40, fjorten 14; sytti 70, sytten 17. Big numbers often go in hundreds: 1300 is «tretten hundre». Phone numbers are read in small groups.

contrasts.title: Common verbs change their vowel in the past
contrasts.body: Regular verbs add -et or -te: jobbe → jobbet, lære → lærte. The verbs you use most are irregular, and the past form has to be learned: gå → gikk, ta → tok, se → så (har sett), bli → ble, være → var. Norwegian uses «har» + past participle much like English: «Jeg har aldri sett så mye snø».

contrasts.title: synes, tror or tenker?
contrasts.body: Use «synes» for an opinion from your own experience: «Jeg synes filmen var bra». Use «tror» when you are not sure: «Jeg tror det blir sol». «Tenker» is about the act of thinking: «Jeg tenker på deg».

contrasts.title: da or når?
contrasts.body: Both mean «when». Use «da» for one single time in the past: «Den startet ikke da jeg prøvde på søndag». Use «når» for the present, the future and things that happen again and again: «Når jeg kommer hjem, lager jeg mat».

contrasts.title: «Takk for sist»
contrasts.body: Norwegians thank you the next time they see you, or in the next message: «Takk for sist» means «thanks for the last time we met». Leaving it out can feel a bit cold.

contrasts.title: Going to dinner at a Norwegian home
contrasts.body: Arrive on time, take your shoes off at the door, and bring something small such as flowers, chocolate or a bottle of wine. The next time you meet, say «Takk for sist».

contrasts.title: «Jeg har jobbet der i fire år»
contrasts.body: For something that started in the past and is still going on, Norwegian uses «har» + past participle with «i»: «Jeg har bodd i Oslo i to måneder». English would say «for two months».

itemNotes.a2-fdw-02: «Sjef» looks like «chef», but it means boss.
itemNotes.a2-fdw-03: «Halv tolv» is half an hour before twelve: 11:30.
itemNotes.a2-fdw-11: After the verb, use the object pronoun: jeg (I) → meg (me).
itemNotes.a2-fdw-13: The sentence starts with «I dag», so the verb «er» comes next, then the subject «det».
itemNotes.a2-fdw-15: After «fordi» (because) the order is subject, then verb: «kollegene er».
itemNotes.a2-flat-01: «Toroms» means two rooms in total: the living room and one bedroom.
itemNotes.a2-flat-02: «Strøm er ikke inkludert»: electricity is not included, so you pay it on top.
itemNotes.a2-flat-11: The sentence starts with «Neste måned», so the verb «vil» comes next, then «jeg».
itemNotes.a2-flat-12: After «fordi» the order is subject, then verb: «den er».
itemNotes.a2-trip-02: From Monday 3 March to Friday 14 March is two working weeks.
itemNotes.a2-trip-06: «Står fast» means is stuck, not standing fast.
itemNotes.a2-trip-09: «Komme for sent» means to be late.
itemNotes.a2-trip-12: After «fordi», «ikke» goes before the verb: «trikken ikke går».
itemNotes.a2-sick-05: «God bedring!» is what you say to someone who is ill: get well soon.
itemNotes.a2-sick-06: In Norway you can usually report yourself sick for a few days. After that you need a note from a doctor, a «sykmelding».
itemNotes.a2-sick-08: «Time» here means an appointment. «En time» can also mean an hour.
itemNotes.a2-sick-10: «Så» here means so, as a result: «Jeg er syk, så jeg blir hjemme».
itemNotes.a2-sick-11: «I morgen» comes first, so the verb «kommer» moves before «jeg».
itemNotes.a2-bid-02: A D-nummer is a temporary ID number for people who stay in Norway for a shorter time. Skatteetaten gives it out after an ID check.
itemNotes.a2-tax-04: Without a tax card, the employer must take 50% tax. Order the tax card before your first payday.
itemNotes.a2-doc-03: «Halv to» is half an hour before two: 13.30.
itemNotes.a2-doc-05: 113 is for medical emergencies. 116 117 (legevakt) is for urgent help when your fastlege is closed.
itemNotes.a2-lunch-04: Kantina is the workplace canteen. Many Norwegians bring a matpakke instead.
itemNotes.a2-nav-02: «Hver fjortende dag» means every 14 days, so every two weeks.
itemNotes.a2-finn-05: «Førstemann til mølla» means first come, first served: whoever comes first gets it.
itemNotes.a2-dug-05: A dugnad is unpaid shared work for the building, the school or the sports club. People expect neighbours to join.
itemNotes.a2-job-03: «Fast stilling» is a permanent job; «midlertidig» is temporary.
itemNotes.a1-abc-04: å sounds like the aw in «law». Norwegian o is closer to «oo».
itemNotes.a1-abc-08: «bær» (berry) has æ. «ber» (asks) has a closed e, like the a in «bay».
itemNotes.a1-abc-09: «hår» means hair, «hør» means listen, «her» means here.
itemNotes.a1-snd-01: kjøre (drive) starts with the soft kj hiss. gjøre (do) starts with a y sound, and skjøre (fragile) with «sh».
itemNotes.a1-snd-02: gj is just a y sound: «yøre».
itemNotes.a1-snd-04: skjære (cut) starts with «sh». kjære (dear) starts with the soft kj hiss.
itemNotes.a1-snd-07: Double n, short vowel: «penn» is a pen. «pen» means pretty.
itemNotes.a1-snd-08: The h in hv- is silent: «hva» sounds like «va».
itemNotes.a1-snd-09: The d at the end of «god» is silent: «go».
itemNotes.a1-hei-08: If the sentence starts with «Nå», the verb still comes second: Nå bor jeg.
itemNotes.a1-hei-09: «I like måte» means likewise. It is the usual answer to «Hyggelig å hilse på deg».
itemNotes.a1-hei-10: «Bare hyggelig» is how you say «you’re welcome».
itemNotes.a1-help-04: «ikke» comes right after the verb: Jeg forstår ikke.
itemNotes.a1-num-11: Today people say «førtini» (49), tens first, as in English.
itemNotes.a1-num-12: Phone numbers are read in groups, digit by digit or in pairs.
itemNotes.a1-shop-08: «Trenger du pose?» Do you need a bag? Bags cost a few kroner extra.
itemNotes.a1-cafe-07: «Kan jeg få …?» Can I have …? is the polite way to order.
itemNotes.a1-cafe-08: «Hva skal det være?» What will it be? is what staff say when it is your turn.
itemNotes.a1-cafe-10: «svart» is black: coffee with nothing in it.
itemNotes.a1-tid-07: If the sentence starts with «Onsdag», the verb comes next: Onsdag passer fint.
itemNotes.a1-tid-09: «Halv ni» is half an hour before nine: 8.30.
itemNotes.a1-tid-10: «Kvart over fire» is a quarter past four: 4.15.
itemNotes.b1-hg-12: «Takk for sist» thanks someone for the last time you met.
itemNotes.b1-ll-04: Ahmed is home after four on weekdays and all day on Saturday, so ten o’clock on a Tuesday doesn’t work.
itemNotes.b1-ll-07: One single time in the past takes «da», not «når».
itemNotes.b1-tm-07: «slik at» (so that) gives the purpose. In speech, «så» is common too.
itemNotes.b1-tm-09: After «fordi», «ikke» comes before the verb: fordi jeg ikke er frisk.
itemNotes.b1-ap-05: «synes» is for an opinion based on your own experience.
itemNotes.b1-bh-07: When a «hvis» clause comes first, the verb of the main clause follows straight after it.
itemNotes.a2-apo-03: «Hver tredje time» means every three hours.
itemNotes.a2-apo-08: When the «hvis» clause comes first, the verb follows straight after it: …, bør du gå til legen.
itemNotes.a2-pak-06: -s after the infinitive makes it passive: hente → hentes (be picked up).
itemNotes.a2-vaer-05: A favourite Norwegian saying: with the right clothes you can be outside in any weather.
itemNotes.a2-inv-05: «Jeg kommer gjerne» = I’d love to come.
itemNotes.a2-inv-06: «ha lyst til» = want to, feel like.
itemNotes.a2-inv-08: «Dessverre» comes first, so the verb comes next: Dessverre kan jeg…
itemNotes.a2-intv-06: «har jobbet … i fire år»: started in the past and still true.

canDo.A1-R-01: I can recognise familiar words, names and numbers on signs, labels and price tags.
canDo.A1-R-02: I can follow very short, simple texts and dialogues about everyday needs.
canDo.A1-L-01: I can hear the difference between Norwegian sounds, including æ, ø and å.
canDo.A1-L-02: I can understand numbers, prices, days and times when people speak slowly.
canDo.A1-L-03: I can understand simple questions in a shop or café when people speak slowly.
canDo.A1-W-01: I can write familiar words and short everyday phrases.
canDo.A1-W-02: I can write a few sentences about myself: my name, where I come from and where I live.
canDo.A1-S-01: I can greet people, introduce myself, say thank you and sorry, and say I don’t understand.
canDo.A1-S-02: I can ask for things in a shop or café and talk about prices and times.
canDo.A2-R-01: I can read short, simple texts about everyday life and work.
canDo.A2-R-02: I can find what I need in notices, timetables, menus and ads.
canDo.A2-R-03: I can understand short messages and simple instructions at work.
canDo.A2-L-01: I can follow everyday words and phrases about me and my work when people speak slowly.
canDo.A2-L-02: I can get the main point of short messages and announcements.
canDo.A2-W-01: I can write short notes and messages about what I need.
canDo.A2-W-02: I can write simple sentences about myself and my work, joined with og, men and fordi.
canDo.A2-S-01: I can introduce myself and answer simple questions about my work and background.
canDo.A2-S-02: I can greet, thank, apologise and invite in short conversations.
canDo.A2-S-03: I can ask for and give directions and practical information.
canDo.B1-R-01: I can understand clear factual texts on topics I know.
canDo.B1-R-02: I can understand what people describe in letters and messages: events, feelings, wishes.
canDo.B1-L-01: I can follow the main points of clear speech at work and in daily life.
canDo.B1-L-02: I can follow the main points of the news on familiar topics when it is spoken clearly.
canDo.B1-W-01: I can write a short, connected text on a familiar topic.
canDo.B1-W-02: I can write emails and messages about my experiences.
canDo.B1-S-01: I can handle most everyday and work situations, like appointments and services.
canDo.B1-S-02: I can give reasons for my opinions and plans.

du.hook: Norwegians say «du» to almost everyone, even the boss.

min.hook: The possessive usually comes after the noun: «sjefen min».

et.hook: Learn each noun with its article: et møte, en jobb.

vaere.hook: «Er» is the same for everyone: jeg er, du er, vi er.

skulle.hook: «Jeg skal» is the everyday way to talk about plans.

a.hook: «Å» marks the infinitive, like «to» in «to work».

pa.hook: Areas of a city take «på»: på Tøyen, på Storo.

takk.hook: Norwegians say «takk» a lot: takk for maten, takk for i dag.

morgen.hook: «I morgen» means tomorrow, «om morgenen» in the morning.

halv.hook: «Halv tolv» is 11:30: half way to twelve.

mandag.hook: Days are written with a small letter.

hete.hook: «Jeg heter…» is how you say your name.

ga.hook: Buses and trams «går»: they go, they run.

lunsj.hook: Norwegians eat lunch early, often around 11:30.

sjef.hook: Not a cook! A cook is «en kokk».

beskjed.hook: «Takk for beskjed» = thanks for letting me know.

hilsen.meaning: greeting; «Hilsen» = regards (at the end of a message)

toromsleilighet.meaning: two-room flat (living room and one bedroom)

strom.hook: «Strøm» is also a stream: electricity flows.

vondt.meaning: pain; «ha vondt i» = to have a pain in

time.hook: Not «time»! «En time» is an hour or an appointment.

den.meaning: it; the, that (for en and ei words)

foer.hook: før (before) is not for (for): the ø matters.

bo.hook: bo = live in a place; leve = be alive.

ringe.hook: Like ring: you ring someone up.

tid.hook: tid is time in general; a doctor’s «time» is an appointment.

prove.hook: Like prove: you try something out.

bankid.hook: You log in to banks, Helsenorge and Skatteetaten with it.

fodselsnummer.hook: fødsel (birth) + nummer: it starts with your date of birth.

skatteetaten.hook: skatt (tax) + etat (agency). It also gives out ID numbers.

skattekort.hook: It tells your employer how much tax to take from your pay.

legevakt.hook: Call 116 117 when your fastlege is closed.

gjerne.meaning: gladly; vil gjerne = would like to
gjerne.hook: «Jeg vil gjerne…» is the polite way to ask for something.

hytte.hook: «På hytta» is the classic Norwegian weekend.

ski.hook: gå på ski = go skiing (literally walk on skis).

matpakke.hook: Open sandwiches wrapped in paper: the Norwegian lunch.

var-season.hook: Same spelling as «vår» (our): context tells them apart.

meldekort.meaning: employment status form (sent to NAV every two weeks)

fjortende.meaning: fourteenth; hver fjortende dag = every two weeks

hente.hook: «kan hentes» = can be picked up (-s makes it passive).

forstemann.hook: Literally: first man to the mill.

soke.hook: søke på en jobb = apply for a job.

dugnad.hook: Neighbours or parents work together for free, then share food.

journal.hook: Not a newspaper: a patient’s record.

vennlig.hook: «Med vennlig hilsen» = kind regards, at the end of a letter.

kjenne.hook: kjenne is for people and things you know; vite is for facts.

hvor.hook: The h in hv- is silent: «vor».

hyggelig.hook: «Bare hyggelig!» is how you say «you’re welcome».

bra.hook: «Ha det bra!» or just «Ha det!» = bye!

stasjon.hook: The sj sound is spelled «sj» here: «sta-shon».

kino.hook: k before i sounds soft, like kj.

penn.hook: Double n, short vowel. «pen» with one n means pretty.

forti.hook: -ti is the tens, -ten the teens: førti 40, fjorten 14.

tusen.hook: «Tusen takk» = a thousand thanks: thank you very much.

mye.meaning: much, a lot; «hvor mye» = how much

passe.hook: «Det passer fint» = that works for me.

pose.hook: Bags cost extra at the checkout, so the cashier asks.

kontant.hook: Most people in Norway pay by card or phone, so you will mostly answer «kort».

slik.meaning: so, like this; «slik at» = so that

lur.meaning: clever; «det er lurt» = it’s a good idea

klem.meaning: hug (also to sign off a message)

trackSummaries.from-zero: Start from zero: the letters and sounds of Norwegian, saying hello, numbers and prices, the shop, the café and telling the time.
trackSummaries.towards-b1: The next step: talking about what you did, writing to your landlord, meeting minutes, a yearly review at work, a kindergarten letter and a news text about Easter.
trackSummaries.everyday-oslo: Everyday errands and social life: the pharmacy, picking up a parcel, weather and clothes, a dinner invitation, booking a haircut and a job interview.

lessonSummaries.a1-alphabet: Meet the three extra letters æ, ø and å, hear how they differ from a, e and o, and write your first Norwegian words.
lessonSummaries.a1-sounds: Practise the sounds that trip up beginners: kj and sj, long and short vowels, and letters you write but do not say.
lessonSummaries.a1-hello: Say hello, give your name, say where you come from and where you live, and answer the polite phrases people use when they meet you.
lessonSummaries.a1-not-understand: The phrases that keep a conversation going when you are lost: ask someone to repeat or slow down, ask what a word means, and ask the way.
lessonSummaries.a1-numbers: Count from zero to a hundred, understand prices and phone numbers, and haggle a little over a second-hand bike.
lessonSummaries.a1-supermarket: Get through the supermarket checkout in Norwegian: bags, card or cash, the receipt, and the friendly goodbye.
lessonSummaries.a1-cafe: Order a coffee and a cinnamon bun, choose a size, say whether it is to take away, and pay.
lessonSummaries.a1-days-and-time: Learn the days of the week, tell the time, and move a meeting by message. Watch out for «halv ni», which is 8.30.
lessonSummaries.b1-weekend: Read a message about a weekend trip to Holmenkollen and practise the past tense of the verbs you use most.
lessonSummaries.b1-landlord-email: Read an email to a landlord about a broken washing machine, and learn how to describe a problem, ask for help and say when you are available.
lessonSummaries.b1-team-meeting: Read the minutes of a team meeting: a delayed launch, a holiday deadline and new home-office rules. Practise explaining reasons with fordi and slik at.
lessonSummaries.b1-appraisal: Follow a yearly review between Sara and her manager, and practise giving your opinion, saying what you want and explaining why.
lessonSummaries.b1-kindergarten: Read a simplified letter offering a kindergarten place: the deadline to answer, what happens if you miss it, and the settling-in days.
lessonSummaries.b1-easter: Read a news-style text about Easter in Norway: the cabin, skiing, oranges and crime novels, traffic queues and closed shops. Then follow a traffic and weather report.
lessonSummaries.a2-pharmacy: Ask for something for a sore throat at the pharmacy, understand how often to take it, and learn when you need a prescription.
lessonSummaries.a2-parcel: Read a parcel notice: where to pick it up, the pickup code, the deadline and when you need ID. Then follow a message from a courier.
lessonSummaries.a2-weather: Read Sara’s message about her first Oslo autumn, talk about the weather and temperatures, and learn the saying about bad weather and bad clothes.
lessonSummaries.a2-invitation: Read an invitation to dinner from a colleague and the reply, then practise saying yes, no and sorry in a friendly way.
lessonSummaries.a2-hairdresser: Book a haircut by phone: ask what is free, accept another time, give your name, and understand the cancellation rule.
lessonSummaries.a2-job-interview: Follow a job interview at a hotel: talk about your experience and languages, say why you want the job, and ask your own question.
